Fanners
FAN-erz
noun
From fan, the winnowing shovel or basket, from the Latin vannus; a fanner is one who winnows — who tosses the threshed grain into the wind, that the chaff may be carried off and the wheat fall clean upon the floor.

Biblical Definition

A fanner is a winnower. After the threshing, the mingled heap of grain and broken husk was thrown up into the evening wind with a fan — a broad shovel or a basket — and the wind did the sorting: the heavy wheat fell back to the floor, and the light chaff blew away. Mark what the fanner does not do. He makes no difference between wheat and chaff; he only reveals the difference already there. Scripture makes the trade a figure of judgment. Against Babylon the LORD declares, “And will send unto Babylon fanners, that shall fan her, and shall empty her land” (Jer 51:2) — the Medes are His winnowing crew, and the proud city is the heap upon the floor. Against His own people He says, “And I will fan them with a fan in the gates of the land” (Jer 15:7). And He puts the fan into His people’s hand against their enemies: “Thou shalt fan them, and the wind shall carry them away” (Isa 41:16). All of it gathers into John the Baptist’s word concerning Christ: “Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Mat 3:12). The fan is already in His hand. The floor He purges is His own — the visible church, wheat and chaff lying together in one heap through all the season, until the wind of His judgment parts them for ever.

Webster 1828 Definition

Winnowers; those who toss threshed grain into the wind with a fan, that the chaff may blow away and the wheat fall clean.

FANNER, one who fans or winnows grain; a winnower.

From fan, the winnowing shovel or basket, Latin vannus.

He throws the threshed heap into the wind; the chaff blows off, the wheat falls.

He makes no difference between wheat and chaff, but reveals it.

The LORD sends fanners unto Babylon, to fan her and empty her land (Jer 51:2).

Key Scripture

Jer 51:2 — "And will send unto Babylon fanners, that shall fan her, and shall empty her land: for in the day of trouble they shall be against her round about."

Jer 15:7 — "And I will fan them with a fan in the gates of the land; I will bereave them of children, I will destroy my people, since they return not from their ways."

Isa 41:16 — "Thou shalt fan them, and the wind shall carry them away, and the whirlwind shall scatter them: and thou shalt rejoice in the LORD, and shalt glory in the Holy One of Israel."

Mat 3:12 — "Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire."

Modern Corruption

Not a contested doctrine but the winnower’s trade; it recovers the fan already in Christ’s hand and the parting of wheat from chaff upon His own floor.

expand to see more

The word rebukes an age that has quietly retired the doctrine of judgment. Jeremiah’s fanners come to Babylon and empty her land; John says the fan is already in the hand of Christ, who will throughly purge His floor and burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire. Unquenchable: not a cleansing that ends, not a restoring that finally gathers everything into the garner, but a burning that does not go out. A pulpit that will preach the gathering of the wheat and pass over the burning of the chaff has not softened Christ’s word; it has torn the sentence in half and handed the congregation the half that costs nothing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the winnower’s plain trade, but the principle to recover is where the fanning falls. Christ purges His floor — His own threshing-floor, the visible church, where wheat and chaff have lain in one heap all the season through. The wind comes first not to Babylon but to the house of God. And mark the mercy hidden in the terror: the fan makes no chaff into wheat, and no wheat into chaff. It only discovers what every grain has been since the sowing. The elect are not made safe by the fanning; they are shown to be safe, gathered into the garner by the very wind that carries the husk away.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means winnowers — those who fan threshed grain in the wind to part the chaff from the wheat.

Fanner — from fan, the winnowing shovel, Latin vannus.

It denotes a winnower, one who tosses threshed grain into the wind.

The chaff is carried off; the heavy wheat falls back to the floor.

The LORD sends fanners unto Babylon, that shall fan her (Jer 51:2).

Christ’s fan is in His hand, to throughly purge His floor (Mat 3:12).

Usage

"I will send unto Babylon fanners — the LORD’s winnowing crew against a proud city."

"The fanner makes no chaff into wheat; the wind only discovers what each grain was."

"Whose fan is in his hand: Christ purges His own floor, and the chaff burns unquenchably."
